summary.summary: Westminster took no new long-term borrowing in 2025/26 and debt edged down to £569m (mostly £386m of 2019-arranged forward loans at an average 2.579%, plus £113.6m PWLB and £40m LOBOs), while cash invested fell £157m to £306.3m as internal borrowing funded the capital programme - the council is £483m under-borrowed against a total closing CFR of £1,748m. Investment income came in £11.8m under budget (£29.7m vs £41.5m), a shortfall that flows straight to the revenue account. The Operational Boundary (£605m) was exceeded, with gross debt at £855m, because the A2Dominion lease transaction from April 2025 added £257m of lease liabilities to the CFR after the strategy was set; the statutory Authorised Limit (£1,641m) was not breached. The council retained its Moody's Aa3 rating and holds loans and equity in its wholly-owned housing companies (Westminster Builds), with amounts detailed in the separate Integrated Investment Framework rather than this report.

signals.headline: Cash invested down £157.1m in 2025/26 (£463.4m to £306.3m) as reserves, balances and cash flow funded capital spend; investment income £11.8m under budget
signals.why: The internal-borrowing strategy is consuming the cash pile and its income, and £483m of under-borrowing must eventually be refinanced externally.

signals.headline: £40m of LOBO loans (up to 60-year terms) subject to periodic lender rate re-pricing; the council acknowledges refinancing risk from the lender option and is watching conversion offers
signals.why: A lender call would crystallise refinancing at current rates well above the 2.87% average of the existing book.

signals.headline: Loans and equity investments held in wholly-owned housing companies (Westminster Builds) as over-12-month non-specified investments; amounts not stated in this report but in the Integrated Investment Framework
signals.why: Treasury reserves are lent to housing subsidiaries, so their performance sits behind headline cash figures.

compliance.notes: Scored from the Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27-2030/31 (Cabinet 23 Feb 2026, to Full Council 4 Mar 2026) and its statutory appendices (Annual Investment Strategy, MRP Policy, CIPFA Requirements), together with the standalone Capital Strategy 2026/27-2039/40 which supplied the commercial/proportionality, guarantees and capital-strategy disclosures. Strongest areas: an exemplary liability benchmark (separate GF and HRA charts to 2065 with all four balances), the full prudential-indicator set with GF/HRA splits and reconciliations, a detailed AIS counterparty/creditworthiness policy using data beyond ratings, the MRP policy, code adoption/delegation, and the capital strategy's quantified long-term affordability (£931.961m net cost over 15 years with receipts-volatility sensitivity). Weakest areas: interest-rate risk sets no explicit fixed/variable exposure limits (the one core gap, RISK-02); no sterling-only borrowing statement (BOR-03) and no audit-qualification flag (RPT-05) are absent mandatory items; no derivatives policy; and no PI-08 commercial-income ratio, no paras 51-53 compliance statement, and no explicit at-least-quarterly member monitoring. The Integrated Investment Framework (a separate Cabinet paper, not in this packet) holds further commercial detail; commercial/non-treasury requirements here were scored from the capital strategy and AIS.

gaps.evidence: Cap Strategy s.6.21 (p.10): £42m p.a. income from the £599m / 265-property investment portfolio, and TMSS s.5.16 notes commercial income partially offsets GF financing costs - but no net-commercial-income-to-net-revenue-stream ratio is set as a prudential indicator

Cap Strategy s.8.7 (p.22) paraphrases PC paras 51-53 (must not borrow to invest primarily for yield; commercial activity proportionate to financial capacity, with transparency over risk and sustainability); TMSS s.4.6 sets the three investment purposes - but no explicit compliance statement citing paragraphs 51-53
Cap Strategy s.6.28 (p.13) identifies opportunities to rationalise/repurpose/dispose of surplus assets, and s.6.7/7.20-7.22 use disposal receipts to fund the programme

AIS (p.6-8): counterparty credit-rating minimums and the actual investment schedule are shown, but no aggregate quantitative portfolio-risk indicator (e.g. weighted-average credit score/duration) is presented in the documents read
AIS (p.6,10) classifies pooled funds (Money Market Funds £300m, Ultra Short-Dated Bond Funds £75m, Pooled Property Funds £200m) with limits, but MiFID II professional-client status is not disclosed

news_drafts.headline: Adult Social Care faces £1.8m of identified risks from market cost pressures and provider fee demands
news_drafts.lead: Care market inflation is national but uncontrolled at local level. Provider fee pressure will escalate as more councils enter deficit positions in this area.

news_drafts.headline: Cavendish Car Park disposal yields £25m capital receipt but erases £1.976m annual rental income, now funded from reserves
news_drafts.lead: Trading capital assets for one-off liquidity, while accepting permanent income loss, indicates balance sheet strain and reliance on asset sales.

news_drafts.headline: Reserve drawdown strategy: £9.840m drawn from general fund balances plus £38.025m from earmarked reserves to balance 2026/27 budget
news_drafts.lead: Structural budget gaps are being masked by reserve usage. This is not sustainable and signals underlying revenue pressures remain unresolved.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care faces £1.8m of identified risks from market cost pressures and provider fee demands
findings.detail: While currently forecasting a balanced position, ASC has identified £1.8m of risks from increasingly complex care needs, hospital discharge activity, rising demand, and providers seeking higher fees for high-dependency placements. Market capacity constraints are reducing provider availability.
findings.matters: Care market inflation is national but uncontrolled at local level. Provider fee pressure will escalate as more councils enter deficit positions in this area.
findings.figures: £1.8m identified risks, additional £1m reserve funding for Beachcroft Care Home remedial works
findings.quote: providers seeking higher fees for high-dependency placements and wider market challenges resulting from limited provider capacity

findings.headline: Cavendish Car Park disposal yields £25m capital receipt but erases £1.976m annual rental income, now funded from reserves
findings.detail: Sale completed July 2026 after buyer exercised option early. While the one-off capital receipt of £25m plus £17m deferred benefit supports capital programme, the loss of recurring rental income must be offset from reserves annually, reducing future budget flexibility.
findings.matters: Trading capital assets for one-off liquidity, while accepting permanent income loss, indicates balance sheet strain and reliance on asset sales.
findings.figures: £25m immediate receipt, £17m deferred, £1.976m annual rental income loss
findings.quote: The loss of annual investment rental income for Corporate Property (£1.976m). The loss of rental income is being funded from reserves.

findings.headline: Reserve drawdown strategy: £9.840m drawn from general fund balances plus £38.025m from earmarked reserves to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The council is explicitly relying on reserve depletion to balance the budget. Drawdowns include £6.4m from Temporary Accommodation reserve (as transitional support), £7.263m from Property Reserve (including £1.976m to offset rental income lost after Cavendish Car Park disposal), and £2.5m from Service Design reserve.
findings.matters: Structural budget gaps are being masked by reserve usage. This is not sustainable and signals underlying revenue pressures remain unresolved.
findings.figures: £9.840m general fund balances, £38.025m total earmarked drawdowns, forecast reserves £199.386m by year-end
findings.quote: An equivalent sum of £9.840m is budgeted to come from general fund balances.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant moving into deficit in 2026/27, with 14 of 34 schools (41.2%) in licensed deficit
findings.detail: Westminster schools face falling pupil numbers (primary surplus capacity 22.9% as of October 2025, up from 18.9% in May), while high needs expenditure drives DSG into deficit. Fourteen schools hold revenue balance deficits of 7%+ (well above the 10% threshold triggering DfE action plans). Only six have agreed recovery plans; four schools are unable to produce plans.
findings.matters: School deficits are a future budget liability. The high proportion in deficit signals system-wide financial stress, not isolated issues. DfE oversight imminent.
findings.figures: 14 of 34 schools in deficit (41.2%), 6 with agreed recovery plans, 4 unable to produce plans, £2.254m high needs overspend in 2025/26
findings.quote: The DSG is expected to move into an overall deficit in 2026/27 as a result of high needs expenditure.

findings.headline: Business Rates collection rate fell 2.07% year-on-year to 33.63% due to legislative changes and billing delays
findings.detail: Q1 business rates collection at 33.63% (vs 35.70% prior year) reflects disruption from the 2026/27 Business Rates Reset and significant legislative changes to multipliers and relief schemes effective 1 April 2026. Billing delays followed, with collection rates expected to take time to stabilise.
findings.matters: Collection delays create cash flow uncertainty. Cyber incident compounded the problem, and council cannot forecast when rates will stabilise.
findings.figures: 33.63% collection rate vs 35.70% prior year, 2.07% shortfall
findings.quote: As of June 2026 the business rates collection rate to date is 33.63%, which is 2.07% lower than the same month last year. This reflects the impact of the 2026/27 Business Rates Reset and the implementation of significant legislative changes to the business rates multipliers and relief schemes from 1 April 2026. These reforms have increased the complexity of the annual billing process and have resulted in delays in billing at the start of the financial year.
